chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
title: How bop changed the music, and why he did not like it
summary: He first heard bop in the early Forties at Minton's, found it 'for the birds', and preferred gutbucket jazz you can tap your foot to.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: During this time when you were just gigging, I guess, did you feel that the music had changed a lot?

What do you mean? Oh yes, the music had changed. It started changing when I... The music started changing before I even got with Cootie's band, and that was in the early Forties. It started changing then. They were doing some Bop then, back in them days, with ...(?)... thing, and in Minton's Bar. Different ones would be playing their horns -- Dizzy and different ones. They'd come up with some funny passages and things, and it would sound real funny to me. Believe me, it sounded from way out, you know! But it was altogether different. And somebody liked it! Especially the musicians liked it; the young musicians liked it. Yeah, I could see the different right then and there. The music changed immensely.
But Bop was never anything that you liked.

I didn't particularly care for it. No, I never tried to play it. In fact, I don't know if I could play it. I made some Bop passages, one-thing-and-another, but I never went much for the style. I didn't particularly

care for it. I like the old gutbucket Jazz, something you can pat your feet to, you know. Nothing somebody had to drop a bomb, BUMP, DE-DO-DE-BUMP-DE, [SINGS BIRD-LIKE PASSAGE] No, for the birds. Charlie did it, Yardbird.
Well, I guess the rhythms changed, the drumming changed.

Well, if you can call that drumming. They'd just hit anywhere. Just drop a bomb anywhere. BUMP! It's no beat. I mean, I like it solid. No beat. But that's their style of music, and it's become popular. I guess.
